tutorial.title: Checking the Status
tutorial.descriptionContent: Check API responses and use returned JSON data.
tutorial.shortDescriptionContent: Python learners who can send public GET requests

lessons.title: Intro
lessons.interactiveContent:
When we make an API call with requests, we get a response object back. We typically store it in a variable called response.

Make sure to pick response, followed by response.
lessons.hardModeContent:
When we make an API call with requests, we get a response object back. We typically store it in a variable called response.

Store the GET result in response, then parse its JSON data.

Make sure to pick response, followed by get, response, and finally json.

lessons.title: Intro - Copy
lessons.interactiveContent:
We’ve already seen that we can call the json() function to convert the response data into Python data we can work with.

Make sure to pick response, followed by response.
lessons.hardModeContent:
We’ve already seen that we can call the json() function to convert the response data into Python data we can work with.

Make sure to pick json, followed by data.

lessons.interactiveContent:

lessons.hardModeContent:

lessons.title: Response Status Codes
lessons.interactiveContent:
Every API response includes a status code that summarizes what happened.

Access it via response.status_code.

Make sure to pick response, followed by .status_code.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Every API response includes a status code that summarizes what happened.

Access it via response.status_code.

Parse the response, read its status separately, and print the parsed data.

Make sure to pick json, followed by response, .status_code, and finally data.

lessons.title: Response Status Codes - Copy
lessons.interactiveContent:
Just like the data from response.json(), we can save the value of response.status_code in a variable.

Make sure to pick status, followed by =.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Just like the data from response.json(), we can save the value of response.status_code in a variable.

Parse the response into data. Store the status code in status.

Make sure to pick json, followed by status, =, and finally status_code.

lessons.title: A Successful Response
lessons.interactiveContent:
When we make a GET request, a status code of 200 means the request succeeded.

Check whether the status code, saved in status, equals 200.

Make sure to pick status, followed by ==, and finally 200.
lessons.hardModeContent:
When we make a GET request, a status code of 200 means the request succeeded.

Compare status on the left with the success code on the right.

Make sure to pick get, followed by status_code, status, ==, and finally 200.

lessons.interactiveContent:

Make sure to pick status_code.
lessons.hardModeContent:

Make sure to pick status_code.

lessons.interactiveContent:
Complete the comparison that checks for a successful GET response.

Make sure to type 200.

lessons.interactiveContent:
Use the successful status check before working with the forecast.

Make sure to pick == 200.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Run this branch only when the response has the successful GET status code.

Make sure to pick status_code, followed by ==, and finally 200.

lessons.interactiveContent:
Recall the response attribute that contains the status code.

Make sure to pick status_code.
lessons.hardModeContent:

Make sure to pick status_code.

lessons.interactiveContent:
A map app sends another GET request. Complete its successful response check.

Make sure to pick ==, followed by 200.
lessons.hardModeContent:
A map app sends another GET request. Complete its successful response check.

lessons.title: Choose the Safe Check
lessons.interactiveContent:
Which condition makes the program use data only after a successful GET response?

response.status_code == 200response.status_code == 404response.status_code = 200

response.status_code == 200.
lessons.hardModeContent:
A GET response has status 404 instead of the expected success code.

Which valid condition is false, so the program skips using the data?

response.status_code == 200response.status_code == 404response.status_code != 200

response.status_code == 200.

lessons.title: When Data Never Arrives
lessons.interactiveContent:
So far, our API calls have always been successful. But that won’t always be the case.

Handling errors helps our program respond clearly when an API request doesn’t go as expected.

lessons.title: Two Sides of Failure
lessons.interactiveContent:
APIs can return different errors when something goes wrong. Let’s start with 404, which means the requested resource could not be found.

Make sure to pick ==, followed by 404.
lessons.hardModeContent:
APIs can return different errors when something goes wrong. Let’s start with 404, which means the requested resource could not be found.

Print the message only when the requested resource was not found.

Make a GET request for the missing Pokémon at url.

Make sure to pick get, followed by status_code, ==, and finally 404.

lessons.title: A Missing Resource
lessons.interactiveContent:
A Not Found response with status 404 means the server can't find the requested resource, such as a Pokémon with the name Mimo.

Make sure to pick response followed by .status_code and then ==, 404.
lessons.hardModeContent:
A Not Found response with status 404 means the server can't find the requested resource, such as a Pokémon with the name Mimo.

Fetch the resource and show the message only for a Not Found response.

Make sure to pick get, followed by response, .status_code, ==, and finally 404.

lessons.title: Handle a 404
lessons.interactiveContent:
When we check for 404, we can show a clear message when the requested resource doesn't exist.

Make sure to pick print, followed by "Pokémon not found".
lessons.hardModeContent:
When we check for 404, we can show a clear message when the requested resource doesn't exist.

Print Pokémon not found only for a Not Found response.

Make sure to pick status_code, followed by ==, 404, print, and finally "Pokémon not found".

lessons.title: A Server Problem
lessons.interactiveContent:
An Internal Server Error response with status 500 means the server failed while handling a valid-looking request.

Make sure to pick 500.
lessons.hardModeContent:
An Internal Server Error response with status 500 means the server failed while handling a valid-looking request.

Keep the missing-resource and server-error branches separate, then parse responses with neither known error.

Make sure to pick 404, followed by 500, and finally json.

lessons.title: Handle a 500
lessons.interactiveContent:
We can respond differently to missing resources and server failures.

Add an elif branch so the app can respond differently.

Make sure to pick elif followed by response and then ., status_code, ==, 500.
lessons.hardModeContent:
We can respond differently to missing resources and server failures.

After handling missing resources, report only server errors in the next branch. Parse data only when neither error occurs.

Make sure to pick elif, followed by response, ., status_code, ==, and finally 500.

lessons.title: Handle Errors First
lessons.interactiveContent:
We can call response.json() in the final branch so the app reads product data only when neither known error occurred.

Make sure to pick else, followed by :.
lessons.hardModeContent:
You already have a response. Parse its JSON data only when neither known error occurred, then print the data.

Make sure to pick else, followed by response, json, and finally data.

lessons.hardModeContent:

lessons.title: More Than One Success
lessons.interactiveContent:
We’ve seen that a 200 status code means a request succeeded. For POST requests, a successful creation often returns 201 instead.

A profile API returns 201 after creating a profile. A check for only 200 calls this successful request a failure.

lessons.title: Meet response.ok
lessons.interactiveContent:
The response.ok property is True for status codes below 400 and False for 400- and 500-level errors.

Using response.ok is an easier and safer way to deal with errors than checking the status_code directly.

Make sure to pick response, followed by ., and finally ok.

lessons.title: Check Any Success
lessons.interactiveContent:
We use response.ok as the condition for any response from requests that is considered successful and can provide data.

Make sure to pick response, followed by ., and finally ok.
lessons.hardModeContent:
You can use response.ok as a condition because it gives a Boolean result, unlike the numeric status code.

Use the general response check to print success for statuses below 400, including 201.

Retrieve the airport at url with a GET request before checking its response.

Make sure to pick get, followed by url, response, and finally ok.

lessons.title: Handle a Failed Check
lessons.interactiveContent:
The else branch now handles every 400- or 500-level response instead of listing each error code.

Make sure to pick if, followed by else.
lessons.hardModeContent:
The else branch now handles every 400- or 500-level response instead of listing each error code.

Make sure to pick if, followed by response, ok, and finally else.

lessons.title: Handle a Failed Check - Copy
lessons.interactiveContent: We can then safely unpack the response data.

lessons.title: Raise HTTP Errors
lessons.interactiveContent:
The response.raise_for_status() method raises an HTTPError for 400- and 500-level responses. Successful responses continue.

Make sure to pick response, followed by .raise_for_status().
lessons.hardModeContent:
The response.raise_for_status() method raises an HTTPError for 400- and 500-level responses. Successful responses continue.

Check for HTTP errors before parsing the response data.

Send a GET request for the nonexistent airport at url, then validate the response.

Make sure to pick get, followed by response, raise_for_status, and finally json.

lessons.interactiveContent:

Make sure to pick get(url).
lessons.hardModeContent:
We can use try and except with raise_for_status() to catch HTTP errors and handle failed API requests.

Add requests.exceptions.HTTPError to catch the HTTPError.

Make sure to pick requests, followed by .exceptions, and finally .HTTPError.
lessons.hardModeContent:
In the except block, we chain the exception type to catch HTTP errors specifically.

Add requests.exceptions.HTTPError to catch the HTTPError.

Make sure to pick raise_for_status, followed by except, requests, .exceptions, and finally .HTTPError.

lessons.title: Check Before JSON
lessons.interactiveContent:
Call response.raise_for_status() before response.json(). An HTTP error then stops normal processing before the app reads data.

Make sure to pick response, followed by .raise_for_status().
lessons.hardModeContent:
Stop on HTTP errors before parsing the response's JSON data, so an error prevents normal processing.

Make sure to pick response, followed by raise_for_status, response, and finally json.
